werk/tina-turner-acid-queen.text:
Acid Queen is Tina Turner's second solo album, released in 1975 by EMI in Great Britain and by United Artists in the United States. It is her last solo record before the break with Ike. The title comes from her role as the Acid Queen in Ken Russell's film Tommy, based on the rock opera by The Who. She recorded two different versions of the song, one for the film and one for this album.

The first side consists of rock covers: Under My Thumb and Let's Spend the Night Together by the Rolling Stones, I Can See for Miles by The Who and Whole Lotta Love by Led Zeppelin. The second side was largely written and produced by Ike Turner, and includes Baby Get It On, the last single by Ike & Tina together. Billboard praised the production, but Dave Marsh of Rolling Stone thought the arrangements were unwisely chosen.
werk/tina-turner-acid-queen.listen: Listen to Whole Lotta Love and compare it with Led Zeppelin's original: according to AllMusic, this version turns the dynamics of the original upside down.

werk/tina-turner-love-explosion.text:
Love Explosion came out at the end of 1979 and is Tina Turner's fourth solo album. It was her second since she left Ike Turner and the Ike and Tina Turner Revue. She recorded it mainly in London, while the horns were recorded in New York. The producer was Alec R. Costandinos, a major name in French disco. The album shows strong funk and disco influences. It was not released in the United States.

Two soul ballads appear on the record: I See Home and Just a Little Lovin', a song previously recorded by Dusty Springfield. Backstabbers is a mid-tempo version of the 1972 soul classic by The O'Jays. Love Explosion was released as a single in Australia, Music Keeps Me Dancin' in Europe. Because the record failed to chart, United Artists parted ways with her. Private Dancer followed in 1984.
werk/tina-turner-love-explosion.listen: Listen to Backstabbers, a mid-tempo cover of a soul classic, and notice how much calmer the tempo is than on a disco record.

werk/tina-turner-private-dancer.text:
After her split from Ike Turner, Tina Turner struggled to get a solo career off the ground. In 1983, Capitol A&R man John Carter signed her, despite resistance within the label. Private Dancer was her first album for Capitol. Four production teams worked on it, including Rupert Hine and Martyn Ware of Heaven 17, in various studios in England.

The sound was a break with the rhythm and blues of her years with Ike. The record mixes up-tempo songs and ballads from pop and rock, with a touch of smooth jazz and contemporary R&B. The title song was written by Mark Knopfler and features a guitar solo by Jeff Beck. Terry Britten produced What's Love Got to Do with It, which has a reggae tinge. Critics praised her raw but powerful voice and saw a strong comeback. It became a worldwide success and won four Grammys. The New York Times called it a milestone in the development of pop-soul.
werk/tina-turner-private-dancer.listen: Listen to Private Dancer and notice how her voice keeps cutting through the glossy production, and wait for Jeff Beck's guitar solo.

werk/tina-turner-tina-turns-the-country-.text:
Tina Turns the Country On! is Tina Turner's first solo album, released in September 1974 on United Artists. She made it while she was still part of the Ike & Tina Turner Revue. Her husband Ike Turner wanted to introduce her to a wider audience this way. The record was made at their own studio, Bolic Sound in Inglewood, California, and produced by the Nashville producer Tom Thacker.

Almost everything is covers of country and folk artists, among them Kris Kristofferson, Bob Dylan, Olivia Newton-John, James Taylor and Dolly Parton. Only Bayou Song was written especially for her, by Peter-John Morse. No singles were released. The record did not chart, but earned a Grammy nomination for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance. Billboard called it a fine mix of country, folk and soft rock and praised her singing. The album did not appear digitally until November 2023.
werk/tina-turner-tina-turns-the-country-.listen: Listen to Bayou Song, the only track on the album written especially for her, and compare it with the covers.

werk/tito-puente-dance-mania.text:
Dance Mania is a 1958 studio album by the American musician Tito Puente. He leads the orchestra, writes the arrangements and plays timbales, vibraphone and marimba. The ensemble includes seven trumpeters and four saxophonists, with Raymond Concepción on piano and Bobby Rodríguez on bass. The percussion is in the hands of Ray Barretto on congas and Ray Rodríguez on bongos. Julito Collazo plays congas on two tracks. Santitos Colón sings the lead vocals and leads the chorus.

The titles show which dance styles are featured: son montuno, mambo, bolero and guaracha. In 2002 the record was added to the National Recording Registry, and it appears on the list of 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.
werk/tito-puente-dance-mania.listen: In El Cayuco (Son Montuno), listen to the percussion and to the interplay between the lead singer and the chorus.

werk/tlc-crazysexycool.text:
After their 1992 debut, the three women began work on a follow-up in 1993, but the recording went slowly because of personal problems. Lisa Left Eye Lopes in particular was struggling, and because she was undergoing treatment at a clinic she could contribute very little. The sessions lasted until September 1994 and took place in studios in Atlanta, Los Angeles and New York, among other places. The group again worked with Dallas Austin, Babyface and Jermaine Dupri, and with newer makers such as Organized Noize and Chucky Thompson. Sean Combs helped with the hip-hop soul.

The record mixes hip-hop beats, funk, deep grooves and smooth production. The lyrics deal with sexuality, romance and youthful optimism, and the record is regarded as a coming-of-age story. Waterfalls touches on violence surrounding the drug trade and on the HIV and AIDS epidemic, and Cee-Lo Green sang backing vocals. CrazySexyCool was well received and is the best-selling album by an American girl group.
werk/tlc-crazysexycool.listen: Listen to Waterfalls and notice what the lyrics say about violence surrounding the drug trade and about the AIDS epidemic.

werk/tom-jones-a-tom-ic-jones.text:
A-Tom-ic Jones is Tom Jones's second album for Decca and his third overall. It was released in 1966. The title is a pun, and the cover shows an atomic explosion in the background. Les Reed was the musical director. In the United States the record appeared with a different cover, without the explosion, because the label did not want to alarm the public.

The tracks differed there too. Four tracks were dropped to make room for two theme songs with which Jones had had success, Thunderball and Promise Her Anything. The repertoire includes Dr. Love, Face of a Loser and More. The reviewer Stephen Thomas Erlewine thought that Jones sings well, but that the material does not suit his performance. He therefore found the album weaker than the first two, and he was not surprised that it had little success.
werk/tom-jones-a-tom-ic-jones.listen: Listen to More and notice how Jones shows off his voice in a calm, melodic song.

werk/tom-jones-along-came-jones.text:
Along Came Jones is the debut album of the Welsh singer Tom Jones. It was released in 1965 and contains his big hit It's Not Unusual. The record reached number 11 on the British album chart and stayed there for five weeks. Some tracks are covers, others were written especially for Jones, such as The Rose by Gordon Mills. The British edition has sixteen tracks.

The title possibly refers to a song of the same name. In June 1965, Parrot Records released a shortened twelve-track version in North America, under the title It's Not Unusual.
werk/tom-jones-along-came-jones.listen: In It's Not Unusual, listen to the power of Jones's voice and notice how confidently he sings.

werk/tom-jones-from-the-heart.text:
From the Heart is Tom Jones's third British album. It was released in 1966 on Decca and consists largely of well-known pop standards. The record was not released in North America. Parrot Records put many of the tracks together on Jones's fourth American album, Green, Green Grass of Home, named after the hit.

On the cover, Jones looks out over Pontypridd, his home town. The photograph was taken on Graig Mountain, on the path above Graig Terrace. The repertoire ranges from Cole Porter and Hoagy Carmichael to Leiber and Stoller and Rodgers and Hammerstein. You can hear Begin the Beguine, Georgia on My Mind, Kansas City and When I Fall in Love. Charles Blackwell, John Scott and Johnny Harris made the arrangements. Bill Price was the recording engineer.
werk/tom-jones-from-the-heart.listen: Listen to Georgia on My Mind and notice how Jones sings a familiar standard with great power in his voice.

werk/tom-jones-what-s-new-pussycat.text:
What's New Pussycat? is Tom Jones's second studio album. It was released to capitalise on the hit with the title song from the film What's New Pussycat?. Remarkably, the record came from his American label Parrot, not from Decca. Peter Sullivan produced, Bill Price was the engineer and Les Reed was the musical director.

The record also contains tracks that had been removed from the American version of his debut, such as I've Got a Heart, The Rose, Some Other Guy and Endlessly. Bama Lama Bama Loo, a hit by Little Richard, had been sung live by him earlier that year on an EP and appears here in a studio version. B-sides of earlier singles make up the rest.
werk/tom-jones-what-s-new-pussycat.listen: In Bama Lama Bama Loo, listen to the vocals and notice the energy that a rock 'n' roll song by Little Richard demands.

werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-dam.text:
Damn the Torpedoes is the third album by Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and was released in October 1979. It came about in the midst of a legal battle. When Petty's record company was sold to MCA, he felt that his contract had lapsed as a result. MCA sued him, Petty declared himself bankrupt, and in the end he signed with Backstreet Records, a subsidiary of MCA. The record was made at Sound City in Van Nuys and Cherokee Studios in Hollywood, with co-producer Jimmy Iovine.

Iovine brought a considerable step forward in the production. The album became the band's first top 10 record and reached number 2 in America; only Pink Floyd's The Wall kept it from first place. Don't Do Me Like That and Refugee became hits. Rolling Stone wrote enthusiastically on its release, and AllMusic later called it one of the great records of the album rock era.
werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-dam.listen: In Refugee, listen to the guitar and the organ and notice how the song sounds both tense and compelling at the same time.

werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-har.text:
Hard Promises is the fourth studio album by Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and was released on 5 May 1981 on Backstreet Records. The working title was Benmont's Revenge, after the keyboard player Benmont Tench. Jimmy Iovine and Petty produced it. Stevie Nicks sings on Insider, a duet, and the title comes from that song's chorus.

The release was delayed by a dispute with the distributor MCA over the price: the label wanted to charge a dollar more than usual. Petty protested in the press, many fans supported him, and in the end MCA dropped the price increase. During the recording sessions John Lennon was supposed to visit the same studio, but he was murdered before the visit. The band had We Love You J.L. engraved in the run-out groove of early pressings. Bassist Ron Blair left the band after this album, which is the last full record with the original line-up.
werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-har.listen: Listen to Insider and notice how the vocals of the duet are divided: when do you hear the second voice?

werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-lon.text:
Long After Dark is the fifth studio album by Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and was released on 2 November 1982 on Backstreet Records. Jimmy Iovine and Petty produced it. It was the first record with Howie Epstein on bass and backing vocals. His voice can be heard throughout the album and from then on became a fixed part of the band's sound.

You Got Lucky became a hit on MTV. Change of Heart, like that song, reached the American top forty, and Straight into Darkness was also released as a single. A number of tracks from the sessions stayed on the shelf for a long time. Two of them, Keep a Little Soul and Keeping Me Alive, did not come out until years later, on the box set An American Treasure, among other places. In 2024 an expanded deluxe edition appeared with twelve live and unreleased tracks.
werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-lon.listen: Listen to You Got Lucky and notice which instrument, besides the vocals, stands out the most.

werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-tom.text:
The debut was released in November 1976 on Shelter Records. The band recorded and mixed it at Shelter Studio in Hollywood. The album received little attention in the United States. Only after a British tour did it climb to number 24 on the British album chart, and Anything That's Rock 'n' Roll became a hit there.

Breakdown was the first single and reached the American top 40. American Girl grew into one of the group's most recognisable songs. After almost a year and many good reviews, the album also reached the American charts in 1978, where it peaked at number 55 and later went gold. Robert Christgau found the songs pleasant and the riffs dynamically performed. The album appears in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.
werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-tom.listen: Listen to Breakdown: notice how the guitars and the organ together carry the beat and how the vocals lie loosely on top of it.

werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-you.text:
The second album was released in May 1978 on Shelter Records. The working title was Terminal Romance. Tom Petty produced it together with Denny Cordell and Noah Shark, and Josh Kosh designed the sleeve. That year the album reached number 23 on the American chart, higher than its predecessor from 1976.

The press was mixed. Many reviewers thought it slightly inferior to the reasonably well-received debut, although Rolling Stone wrote of an impressive stylistic coherence between the two records. The newspaper The Globe and Mail called Petty a pop stylist who plainly repeats the musical and lyrical themes of pop as they were before country rock and disco swamped them.
werk/tom-petty-and-the-heartbreakers-you.listen: Listen to Listen to Her Heart: notice how guitars and piano carry the song and how the chorus leaps out.

werk/tommy-flanagan-overseas.text:
In 1957 the pianist Tommy Flanagan toured Europe as a member of trombonist J.J. Johnson's band. In Stockholm he was given the chance, for the first time, to lead a recording session himself. From Johnson's group he chose bassist Wilbur Little and drummer Elvin Jones. On 15 August the three recorded at Metronome Studio in Stockholm the music that was later released as Overseas. It was his debut as a bandleader.

Six of the nine pieces were written by Flanagan himself. In addition, the trio played Charlie Parker's Relaxin' At Camarillo, Billy Strayhorn's Chelsea Bridge and Willow Weep for Me. Flanagan re-recorded five of these pieces in 1996 for Sea Changes, his last studio album as a leader. The album was released on Prestige Records. The Penguin Guide to Jazz praised his touch and his clear melodic ideas. The label DIW later released all the tracks from the session on The Complete Overseas.
werk/tommy-flanagan-overseas.listen: In Willow Weep for Me, listen to Flanagan's touch: notice how lightly and clearly he lets the melody sound, while bass and drums calmly carry the trio.

werk/tony-williams-life-time.text:
Life Time is the debut of the drummer Tony Williams as a bandleader. He recorded the album in August 1964 for Blue Note, over two days of sessions. He wrote all five tracks himself. He worked with saxophonist Sam Rivers, vibraphonist Bobby Hutcherson, pianist Herbie Hancock and three different bassists: Ron Carter, Gary Peacock and Richard Davis.

Besides drums, Williams also plays timpani, wood blocks, maracas and triangle. The music is unpredictable, and that keeps the listener engaged. The reviewer Scott Yanow called it, in AllMusic, a very strong debut by a masterly drummer. The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings included the record in a list of essential recordings that it calls a core collection.
werk/tony-williams-life-time.listen: Listen to Two Pieces of One: Red: follow Williams's drums and notice how freely they move around Rivers's saxophone.

werk/tony-williams-spring.text:
Spring is the second album by the drummer Tony Williams and was released in 1965 on Blue Note. It was recorded with two tenor saxophonists, Sam Rivers and Wayne Shorter, alongside pianist Herbie Hancock and bassist Gary Peacock. On the five tracks, all by Williams himself, not everyone plays on every piece. Hancock, for example, is absent from the first track, Extras.

Given the talent in the studio, expectations were high. The reviewer Al Campbell felt in AllMusic that it did not become a milestone. The album is not forgotten material, he wrote, but the compositions rarely managed to bring the musicians together into a true unity, which left the session somewhat sloppy.
werk/tony-williams-spring.listen: Listen to Tee, the long closing track: notice how the two saxophonists and the drums interact with each other.

werk/tony-williams-the-joy-of-flying.text:
The Joy of Flying is a fusion album by the drummer Tony Williams, recorded at the end of his Lifetime years. It is regarded as his first solo record since 1966. The record contains three duets, two with Jan Hammer and one with the free-jazz pianist Cecil Taylor, and three different quartets. In one of them Herbie Hancock, Stanley Clarke and Tom Scott on Lyricon played, in another Ronnie Montrose, Brian Auger and Mario Cipollina. On Hip Skip a five-man horn section joins in.

Open Fire comes from a concert on 27 July 1978 in Japan. The Bay State Banner wrote that Williams wove contrasting styles such as rock and R&B into an electric fabric of shifting colours and moods. DownBeat gave four stars: according to the reviewer, Williams is at his best when he picks a side and lets all the rhythm boil.
werk/tony-williams-the-joy-of-flying.listen: Listen to Morgan's Motion and notice how Williams reacts on the drums to Cecil Taylor's piano playing.

werk/toshiko-akiyoshi-her-trio-her-quart.text:
The pianist Toshiko Akiyoshi recorded this album in New York in 1956. It was released on the Storyville label. The sleeve uses art from Joan Miró's Black and Red series. The record consists of two line-ups, a trio and a quartet.

On five tracks she plays with alto saxophonist Boots Mussulli, bassist Wyatt Ruther and drummer Ed Thigpen. On three other tracks she can be heard with bassist Oscar Pettiford and drummer Roy Haynes. The repertoire combines her own work, such as Salute to Shorty and Pea, Bee and Lee, with well-known standards such as All the Things You Are, I'll Remember April and Thou Swell. Kelo was written by J.J. Johnson.
werk/toshiko-akiyoshi-her-trio-her-quart.listen: Listen to Pea, Bee and Lee, a trio piece by the pianist herself, and notice how piano, bass and drums carry the piece together without a horn.

werk/toshiko-akiyoshi-remembering-bud-cl.text:
The pianist Toshiko Akiyoshi recorded this trio album in 1990 as a tribute to the pianist Bud Powell. Almost all the pieces come from Powell himself, such as Cleopatra's Dream, Un Poco Loco and Tempus Fugit. The title piece, Remembering Bud, she wrote herself.

Playing with her are bassists George Mraz and Ray Drummond and drummers Lewis Nash and Al Harewood, depending on the track. The album was released on the Japanese label Nippon Crown and in the United States on Evidence. At nearly ten minutes the title piece is the longest track, and the other tracks mostly last four to seven minutes.
werk/toshiko-akiyoshi-remembering-bud-cl.listen: Listen to Un Poco Loco, a piece by Bud Powell, and notice how piano, bass and drums play together as a trio.

werk/toto-africa.text: In April 1982, Toto IV was released, with Africa and Rosanna. Toto consisted of Los Angeles session musicians who also played on other artists' records, including Michael Jackson's Thriller. Their sound was smooth, perfect and complex. Critics found it soulless, but the album won six Grammys. Years later, through the internet, Africa became one of the best-known songs of the 1980s.
werk/toto-africa.listen: Africa has a percussion rhythm and a synthesizer melody that sounds like a kalimba. Listen for the big, multi-voiced chorus.

werk/toto-hydra.text:
Hydra is Toto's second album and was released in 1979. After the success of the debut, the band did not want to make the same record again and tried something different. Guitarist Steve Lukather later felt that the album may have been made a little hastily. The production was by the band themselves, together with Tom Knox and Reggie Fisher. In 1980, CBS had a video of four songs filmed, for which a New York sewer was built, as also seen on the cover.

The song 99, inspired by the 1971 science-fiction film THX 1138, reached number 26 on the American Hot 100 and was the biggest hit. The record was a commercial success, but far less popular than the debut. Cashbox called it more adventurous than the first album, with excursions into progressive rock. Billboard praised Lukather's guitar playing as breathtaking.
werk/toto-hydra.listen: Listen to St. George and the Dragon and notice how the atmosphere of knights and dragons, a fairy-tale world to escape into, comes back in the music.

werk/toto-turn-back.text:
For their third album, Toto wanted to become an arena rock band with a heavier sound. They worked with Geoff Workman, who had previously worked with Queen. Guitarist Steve Lukather said that Workman gave the album a new sound with almost no midrange. The album was released in January 1981.

Goodbye Elenore became the band's first Japanese hit. Live for Today was the first Toto song that Lukather wrote. In the United States the record disappointed: its highest position was number 41, there were no hits and the band did not tour with it. Columbia threatened to terminate the contract if there was no hit. It came in 1982 with Toto IV. Today Turn Back is a cult favourite among fans.
werk/toto-turn-back.listen: Listen to Live for Today, the first song from Lukather's hand, and notice how solidly it rocks.

werk/toumani-diabate-the-mande-variation.text:
The Mandé Variations was released in 2008 on World Circuit, produced by Nick Gold. Unlike many earlier records by Toumani Diabaté, this album consists entirely of solo kora. The influences range from traditional kora music to modern Western music. It was only his second solo record, twenty years after Kaira from 1988.

Pitchfork noted that here only Diabaté and his kora can be heard, recorded as clearly as possible. The reviewer called the album exceptionally gripping from beginning to end and spoke of the awe that such pure music inspires. The album has eight pieces of between six and more than ten minutes. It was released on 25 February 2008 in the United Kingdom and a day later on Nonesuch Records in the United States.
werk/toumani-diabate-the-mande-variation.listen: Listen to Si Naani, the longest piece, and notice how a single instrument carries all the music.

werk/travis-scott-astroworld.text:
Astroworld is Travis Scott's third album and was released on 3 August 2018. The title refers to the amusement park Six Flags AstroWorld in Houston, which closed in 2005. Scott wanted the album to sound like taking an amusement park away from children. He saw it as a sequel to his debut Rodeo. The recording ran from 2016 to 2018, including with Mike Dean, Hit-Boy, WondaGurl, Tay Keith and Tame Impala. On the cover, photographed by David LaChapelle, a golden inflatable head forms the entrance to an amusement park.

It is a hip-hop and psychedelic rap record with trap. Stargazing was described as psychedelic trap, and Coffee Bean has a funk guitar from old-school hip hop. Sicko Mode, Butterfly Effect, Yosemite and Wake Up were released as singles. The album received glowing reviews, reached number 1 on the Billboard 200 and was nominated for a Grammy for Best Rap Album.
werk/travis-scott-astroworld.listen: Listen to Sicko Mode and notice the switches within the song, where the beat and the mood change several times.

werk/tricky-angels-with-dirty-faces.text:
Angels with Dirty Faces is Tricky's third album, from 1998. The title comes from a film of the same name. Many guests take part: on Broken Homes PJ Harvey sings, on Carriage for Two Scott Ian of Anthrax plays guitar, and on several tracks Marc Ribot's guitar can be heard. The Moment I Feared is a cover of a song by Slick Rick. He produced the album himself, and Martina Topley-Bird sings on a large part of the tracks.

Entertainment Weekly called it his best record since the 1995 debut. According to the reviewer Robert Christgau, it is a rock record with a live band on every track, without samples, with dirty productions that suit the antisocial themes. Later critics felt that at its core it differed little from Pre-Millennium Tension: dub-tinged trip hop, supplemented with rhythms from hardcore hip hop and jungle.
werk/tricky-angels-with-dirty-faces.listen: Listen to Broken Homes and notice the voice of guest singer PJ Harvey.

werk/tricky-juxtapose.text:
Juxtapose is the fourth official studio album by the English musician Tricky. It was released on 16 August 1999 on Island Records, in collaboration with the American producers DJ Muggs and Dame Grease. Guests include the British rapper Mad Dog and D'NA. Kioka Williams sings most of the female vocals, including on the tours that followed.

For Real was the first single, released on 3 August 1999. Contradictive is heard in the film Brokedown Palace, and Scrappy Love in the series Without a Trace. The album reached number 22 in the United Kingdom, number 182 in the United States and number 8 in Norway.
werk/tricky-juxtapose.listen: Listen to Hot Like a Sauna and notice how the guest singers and the rapper take turns.

werk/tricky-maxinquaye.text:
Maxinquaye is Tricky's solo debut, released in 1995. He was dissatisfied with his limited role in Massive Attack and wanted to go his own way. He met the young singer Martina Topley-Bird, who became the main voice on the record. In 1994 he recorded the album, mostly in his own studio in London, together with producer Mark Saunders. The title refers to his late mother Maxine Quaye.

Tricky used techniques from dub and processed samples so heavily that they were barely recognisable any more. He deliberately left glitches and crackles in the mix. The sound is slowed, hazy and fragmented, with elements of hip hop, soul, rock, reggae and ambient techno. The lyrics deal with decay, difficult relationships, fear of intimacy and drug use. Many journalists called the album the best record of the year and the key record of the emerging trip hop.
werk/tricky-maxinquaye.listen: In Ponderosa, listen to the drum loop that carries the whole song. Notice how the beat, the voice and the noise slide over one another.

werk/tricky-pre-millennium-tension.text:
With Pre-Millennium Tension, Tricky wanted to get away from the label trip hop that critics had stuck on his debut Maxinquaye. He said he wanted to make a real punk record, fast and hard, although that did not turn out that way everywhere. The album was released on 11 November 1996 on Island. It was largely recorded at Grove Studios in Ocho Rios in Jamaica and partly in New York, and Ian Caple recorded, mixed and programmed it. According to one reviewer, the move to New York and the work with underground rappers produced a darker sound, with the singles Christiansands, Tricky Kid and Makes Me Wanna Die.

Critics heard ambitious, eclectic and menacing music with influences from ambient, drum and bass, hip hop and dancehall. In 1996 the album placed ninth in the Pazz & Jop poll, and it later made Q magazine's list of the heaviest albums.
werk/tricky-pre-millennium-tension.listen: Listen to Makes Me Wanna Die and notice the sample of To the Listeners by Eric B. & Rakim that is worked into the song.

werk/twarres-wer-bisto.text: In 2000, Wêr bisto was released, by the duo Twarres from the Frisian village of Warga. The song, Frisian for Where are you, became a number 1 hit in the Netherlands and in Flanders. It is so far the only Frisian-language number 1 hit in the Netherlands. A year earlier, the duo had won the audience award with it at Liet, a song festival for songs in regional languages.
werk/twarres-wer-bisto.listen: Hear the clear voice of Mirjam Timmer and see whether you can follow the Frisian.

werk/typhoon-hemel-valt.text: In 2014, the album Lobi da basi by Typhoon, the artist name of Glenn de Randamie, was released. He grew up in 't Harde and began rapping in Zwolle, where a hip-hop scene of its own had grown up around the group Opgezwolle. On Hemel valt, Typhoon combines hip hop with soul and jazz. The album won an Edison. In Nederhop, sound, rhyme and street slang count just as heavily as the beat.
werk/typhoon-hemel-valt.listen: Hear how hip hop, soul and jazz flow into one another, with Typhoon's rap running cheerfully and fast over the beat.

werk/u-roy-dread-in-a-babylon.text:
Dread in a Babylon was released in 1975, when Virgin Records was turning its attention to Jamaican music in the mid-1970s. Tony Robinson produced the album and Errol Thompson was the engineer. The Jamaican musician U-Roy was accompanied by the bands Soul Syndicate and Skin, Flesh & Bones. On the front, his face is hidden behind a cloud of marijuana smoke. Runaway Girl was released as a single.

Trench Town Rock is an instrumental track. His favourite was Chalice in the Palace, in which he imagines smoking marijuana with Queen Elizabeth II. The album was a commercial success in Jamaica and Great Britain, where he promoted it with a tour. The critical response was mixed: Robert Palmer thought it suitable only for the most dedicated reggae fans. AllMusic later counted it among the dub masterworks of the 1970s.
werk/u-roy-dread-in-a-babylon.listen: Listen to Chalice in the Palace: notice how U-Roy's voice moves between talking, shouting and singing, over an unobtrusive backing.

werk/u2-achtung-baby.text:
After the criticism of Rattle and Hum, the band from Dublin felt creatively stuck and looked for new paths. In October 1990 they began at Hansa Studios in Berlin, with Daniel Lanois as producer, Brian Eno as adviser and Flood as engineer. Berlin, after the fall of the Wall, was supposed to inspire them, but the atmosphere in the city was disappointing. The members quarrelled about the direction: Bono and The Edge were listening to electronic dance music and industrial, while Larry Mullen and Adam Clayton preferred the old sound. The group even considered splitting up, until One emerged from an improvisation. The record was then finished in Dublin.

The sound is harder, darker and more ironic than before, with influences from alternative rock, industrial and dance. Achtung Baby received good reviews, topped the American chart and was followed by the Zoo TV Tour.
werk/u2-achtung-baby.listen: Listen to One and notice how calm and restrained the song is, after all the searching for a new sound.

werk/u2-boy.text:
U2's debut album was recorded from July to September 1980 at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin. The band worked for the first time with producer Steve Lillywhite, after the plan with Martin Hannett fell through. Lillywhite loved experiments: he put Larry Mullen Jr.'s drums in a stairwell and recorded broken bottles and cutlery being dragged along a spinning bicycle wheel.

The lyrics deal with growing up, innocence and the transition from boy to man, and that is also the idea behind the sleeve with a boy's face. The Edge plays with echo and long, floating chords instead of blues riffs. I Will Follow, about the early death of Bono's mother, became one of the first U2 songs to be played on American radio. Boy received mostly positive reviews.
werk/u2-boy.listen: Listen to I Will Follow and notice The Edge's guitar: how the echoes carry the riff. Notice, too, how the song keeps moving.

werk/u2-october.text:
October is U2's second record and was released in October 1981. The band recorded it at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin, again with Steve Lillywhite. The sessions were chaotic: in the United States a bag containing Bono's lyrics and ideas had gone missing, and he had to make up many lines on the spot. It also mattered that Bono, The Edge and Larry Mullen Jr. were members of a Christian group, the Shalom Fellowship, and doubted whether faith and rock could go together. That even threatened the band's survival.

That faith resounds in Gloria, with a Latin chorus, and in With a Shout (Jerusalem) and Tomorrow. The Edge uses piano for the first time in songs such as I Fall Down and October. In Tomorrow, a lament for Bono's mother, Uilleann pipes are played. The reviews were mixed.
werk/u2-october.listen: Listen to Tomorrow and notice the Uilleann pipes, the Irish bagpipes, which give the song an almost sad, old-fashioned sound. Can you hear how far that is from the rock guitar in Gloria?

werk/u2-pop.text:
Pop is U2's ninth studio album and was released on 3 March 1997. The recording began in 1995 with producers such as Nellee Hooper, Flood, Howie B and Steve Osborne, who wanted to introduce the band to electronic music and club culture. Drummer Larry Mullen Jr. had a back injury and was unable to play for a while, which forced the others to write their songs in a different way.

The album works with samples, loops, drum machines and sequencers, and builds on the experiments of Achtung Baby and Zooropa. The first single, Discothèque, was strongly electronic. Because the tour had already been booked, time pressure arose and the songs were worked on until the last moment. The band themselves felt the result was unfinished. Pop first received favourable reviews, but in retrospect many regard it as a disappointment.
werk/u2-pop.listen: Listen to Discothèque and notice how loops and dance rhythms play a major role alongside the guitar. Hear what still sounds recognisably like a rock band.

werk/u2-rattle-and-hum.text:
Rattle and Hum is a mixture of live recordings and new studio tracks, released on 10 October 1988 together with a documentary by director Phil Joanou. The album grew out of the Joshua Tree Tour, on which the band immersed themselves in American roots: blues, folk and gospel. Jimmy Iovine produced. Some of the tracks were recorded at Sun Studio in Memphis, where Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash also recorded.

The record opens with a live version of Helter Skelter by the Beatles. In Desire you hear a Bo Diddley beat, in When Love Comes to Town B. B. King plays and sings along, and I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For was recorded live with a gospel choir. The critical response was divided: some critics felt that the band wanted to place itself among its great examples.
werk/u2-rattle-and-hum.listen: Listen to When Love Comes to Town and notice how B. B. King joins in with guitar and vocals in a blues-rock song.

werk/u2-the-joshua-tree.text:
After The Unforgettable Fire, U2 wanted to make a harder-sounding album, within the limits of ordinary song structures. In the 1980s the band had toured the United States for months every year and was fascinated by that country, including American writers and roots music. The producers were Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno. The recording began in January 1986 in Ireland, mainly in two houses, and was finished in November. During the sessions the roadie Greg Carroll died and Bono travelled to Central America, which set the tone of the record.

The lyrics are socially engaged and full of spiritual imagery. With the desert photographs on the sleeve, the group wanted to evoke a cinematic sense of space. With or Without You and I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For became the band's only number 1 singles in the United States. In 1988 the album won a Grammy for Album of the Year and became U2's best-selling record.
werk/u2-the-joshua-tree.listen: Listen to Where the Streets Have No Name, the opening track, and notice how the atmosphere of wide-open space is built up.

werk/u2-the-unforgettable-fire.text:
After the hard-hitting War, the band was afraid of becoming a screaming arena band. They therefore chose a new direction and asked Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois to produce. They also looked for a different place: the recording began in May 1984 at Slane Castle, where the group lived, wrote and recorded. There the band sought the natural reverberation of a large hall. The album was completed in August at Windmill Lane Studios and was released on 1 October 1984. The title refers to an exhibition about the atomic bomb on Hiroshima.

The sound is softer and more atmospheric than before, and Bono described the lyrics as sketches. Pride (In the Name of Love) and MLK are tributes to Martin Luther King. Pride became the band's biggest hit up to that point, and Bad became a favourite in concert. Critics responded generally positively.
werk/u2-the-unforgettable-fire.listen: Listen to MLK, the quiet closing track. Notice how sparse and atmospheric it sounds compared with the harder songs of the previous album.

werk/u2-war.text:
This third album by the Irish band was recorded from September to November 1982 at Windmill Lane Studios in Dublin, with producer Steve Lillywhite. It was released on 28 February 1983. Where the first records were about youth and faith, this one was about war and its consequences. The sound is harder than before, partly because guitarist the Edge used far less echo. Drummer Larry Mullen used a click track for the first time.

Sunday Bloody Sunday opens the album with a military-sounding drum part and a guitar solo that resembles machine-gun fire. The lyrics are about the Troubles in Northern Ireland. New Year's Day took shape under the influence of the Polish movement Solidarność. The record was a great success and reached number one in England, ahead of Michael Jackson's Thriller. It is regarded as U2's first openly political album.
werk/u2-war.listen: Listen to Sunday Bloody Sunday and notice the drum part with which the song begins. Hear how it sounds like a marching rhythm.

werk/u2-zooropa.text:
After Achtung Baby and U2's Zoo TV Tour, Bono and The Edge had a six-month break in 1993 and no desire to rest. In February the band began work on new songs in Dublin, intended as an EP. With Brian Eno and Flood as producers, the project grew into a full album. It was not finished when the tour resumed in May, so the group flew back and forth between Dublin and the concert venues to mix on days off and at night.

The album continues the experiments with alternative rock, electronic dance music and sound effects, with themes such as technology and media overload from the tour. On The Wanderer, Johnny Cash can be heard, who recorded his vocals during a visit to Dublin. Numb, Lemon and Stay (Faraway, So Close!) were released as singles. The reviews were mostly favourable and the album won a Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album. The band themselves have mixed feelings about it.
werk/u2-zooropa.listen: Listen to The Wanderer and notice the voice that carries the song: that of Johnny Cash, who recorded his vocals when he was visiting Dublin.

werk/ultravox-ha-ha-ha.text:
Ha! Ha! Ha! was the band's second album, still Ultravox! at the time, with an exclamation mark as a wink at Neu!. In 1977 the group was led by singer and writer John Foxx. It was released on 14 October 1977 on Island Records, accompanied by the single ROckWrok. It failed to chart, but the label kept believing in the group.

The first album was still strongly influenced by glam rock. This second one is closer to the emerging punk, with songs such as Fear in the Western World and While I'm Still Alive. At the same time, the band used a great deal of synthesizers and electronics for the first time, paid for with the money from the first record. The closing track Hiroshima Mon Amour, with a drum machine, points most clearly ahead to the later synth-pop and remains a favourite with fans and critics. It was the last album with guitarist Stevie Shears.
werk/ultravox-ha-ha-ha.listen: Listen to Hiroshima Mon Amour and notice the drum machine and the synthesizer, which sound like a first sketch of the synth-pop that was to come later.

werk/ultravox-systems-of-romance.text:
Systems of Romance was released on 8 September 1978 on Island Records. It was Ultravox's third album, the last with singer John Foxx and the first without guitarist Stevie Shears. Robin Simon took his place. Conny Plank and Dave Hutchins produced the album, and the influence of Kraftwerk, who also worked with Plank, can be heard. The group used more electronics than ever, with synthesizer bass instead of a regular bass.

The opener Slow Motion immediately revealed the new direction, with rich layers of synthesizer and a guitar with effects. In Quiet Men the regular drum kit is absent and a drum machine provides the rhythm, and Dislocation leans on processed synthesizer sounds. The album received mixed reviews, sold little and failed to chart. Even so, it is regarded as a major influence on the synth-pop of the 1980s. Midge Ure, who later succeeded Foxx, said that he thought the album was great.
werk/ultravox-systems-of-romance.listen: Listen to Slow Motion and notice the synthesizer bass, which here takes the place of a regular bass guitar.

werk/us3-an-ordinary-day-in-an-unusual-p.text:
This third album by the jazz-rap group Us3 was released in 2001. Geoff Wilkinson recorded it in his own home studio. DJ First Rate, Michelob and Alison Crokett contributed. You Can't Hold Me Down was the first single. To promote the record, the group played at the 2001 London Jazz Festival.

The press was glowing. An Australian newspaper called it their most impressive work, in which a simple mix of hip hop, rap and jazz has grown into a funky form of its own. Another paper spoke of a classic blend of jazz and beats, distinctive yet accessible. One reviewer heard calm songs with jazzy beats, a jazzy bass and drums, rap vocals and occasionally instruments from other countries, such as the sitar.
werk/us3-an-ordinary-day-in-an-unusual-p.listen: Listen to You Can't Hold Me Down and notice how jazzy bass and drums go together with rap vocals.

werk/us3-broadway-en-52nd.text:
After the enormous success of the debut Hand on the Torch, Us3 was given a free hand at Blue Note Records. The label's president had the group dig deep into the label's vault and make whatever they wanted there. The second album was released in 1996, and the title refers to an intersection in New York's theatre district, where bebop once had its centre.

The group continued to combine live musicians, samples and hip-hop lyrics. The album sounds darker and more conscious than the debut. Titles such as Caught Up in a Struggle and Doin' a Crime already show this. It was received less well than its predecessor, but it is regarded as a more mature form of jazz rap.
werk/us3-broadway-en-52nd.listen: Listen to Come on Everybody (Get down) and notice how the rap lies over a jazzy backing. Try to hear what sounds live and what seems to be a sample.

werk/usher-8701.text:
8701 is Usher's third album and was released in the summer of 2001 on Arista Records. It was actually supposed to be called All About U and to come out at the end of 2000, but when several tracks leaked on Napster, the release was postponed. The singer recorded new songs in Los Angeles, New York, Minneapolis and Atlanta, including with The Neptunes, Jermaine Dupri and Babyface. The title refers to 1987, when he first sang in church, and to 2001.

His models were Donny Hathaway, Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye and Michael Jackson. The songs are about love and heartbreak. U Remind Me and U Got It Bad both reached number one on the American Hot 100, and U Don't Have to Call reached the top three. Critics praised the singing and the singer's development, although they were less enthusiastic about some of the material.
werk/usher-8701.listen: Listen to U Got It Bad and notice how the vocals carry the theme of love and sorrow.

werk/usher-confessions.text:
Confessions is Usher's fourth studio album and was released on 23 March 2004 on Arista Records. The recording ran from 2003 to 2004. Jermaine Dupri produced many of the tracks, together with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis and Lil Jon, among others. When the album seemed finished, Usher and label boss L.A. Reid felt that one or two songs were still missing. Red Light and Yeah! came out of that.

The title refers to the personal subject matter. Burn is about the end of a relationship, Confessions Part II about a deceitful affair. The album is mainly R&B, with hip hop and crunk running through it, and shows Usher as a crooner. In the first week, 1.1 million copies were sold. The album won a Grammy for Best Contemporary R&B Album and is on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/usher-confessions.listen: Listen to Yeah! and notice how Lil Jon's hard crunk beat contrasts with Usher's smooth vocals.

werk/usher-here-i-stand.text:
Here I Stand was released on 13 May 2008 on LaFace Records. Usher recorded many ballads, inspired by his wife Tameka Foster and his son. Before the recording he had replaced his mother as manager with Benny Medina. In January 2008 his father died, with whom he had had a difficult relationship. The working title was Measure of a Man, but Clay Aiken had already used that name. According to the singer, Here I Stand marked a new chapter in his life.

Six tracks were released as singles. Love in This Club, with Young Jeezy, topped the Billboard Hot 100. Prayer for You is an interlude for his son about the relationship with his own father. Critics saw growth and maturity; others found the style less convincing after Confessions. The album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with 433,000 copies sold in the first week. It also topped the chart in Canada, the United Kingdom and Australia.
werk/usher-here-i-stand.listen: Listen to Prayer for You and notice how the interlude takes the relationship with his own father as the starting point for what he wants to be for his son.

werk/usher-my-way.text:
Usher's 1994 debut album sold modestly, and later he said that it did not suit him. For the follow-up he sought a rawer and more authentic sound and wanted more input of his own. The label LaFace first brought in Dallas Austin, but shelved those recordings. In the end, label boss L.A. Reid sent him to Jermaine Dupri, who became the album's main producer. In addition, Usher worked with Babyface and with Monica and Lil' Kim.

My Way was released in 1997 and became his breakthrough in R&B. The reviews were mostly positive: critics praised his singing and the production, although some found the quality uneven and the record too full of slow songs. Three singles became hits: You Make Me Wanna..., Nice & Slow and the title song. To promote it, he opened for Mary J. Blige and Janet Jackson.
werk/usher-my-way.listen: In Slow Jam, listen to how the voices of Usher and Monica alternate and complement each other in this duet.

werk/van-halen-1984.text:
After Diver Down, guitarist Eddie was dissatisfied: singer David Lee Roth and producer Ted Templeman preferred to keep keyboards small. In 1983 he built his own studio, 5150, and began experimenting there with synthesizers. Here he wrote the new songs without interference from Roth or Templeman. The recording took about three months, whereas the band's earlier records were often finished in less than two weeks.

The result was a mixture of synthesizer songs and the guitar work the group was known for. The short instrumental opener 1984 and the single Jump revolve around the synthesizer. Jump became Van Halen's only number-one hit on the American Hot 100. Panama has a heavy guitar riff and the sound of Eddie's Lamborghini, recorded with microphones at the exhausts. The video for Hot for Teacher got heavy airplay on MTV. The album reached number two in America, behind Michael Jackson's Thriller, and brought the band a broader audience. Roth left in 1985.
werk/van-halen-1984.listen: Listen to Panama and notice the engine sound that comes through between the heavy guitar riff. That is Eddie's car, recorded close to the exhausts.

werk/van-halen-5150.text:
5150 was released on 24 March 1986 on Warner Bros. and is the first album with singer Sammy Hagar, who replaced David Lee Roth. The title refers to Eddie Van Halen's home studio. Producer Ted Templeman had left; Donn Landee took over the production, with Mick Jones of Foreigner as an additional producer. The recording began in November 1985 and was finished in February 1986.

The record contains more love songs and ballads than earlier albums, and the guitar now sits on an equal footing in the mix. It is also the band's first album without instrumental tracks. The first reviews were mixed, but later it came to be seen as one of the group's most complete records. The album reached number one on the Billboard 200.
werk/van-halen-5150.listen: Listen to Why Can't This Be Love and notice how vocals and guitar sit equally strong in the mix. Hear how serious the tone is.

werk/van-halen-diver-down.text:
Diver Down was released on 19 April 1982 on Warner Bros. At the beginning of 1982 the band had recorded (Oh) Pretty Woman as a stand-alone single, and when it became a hit, the record company quickly demanded an album. The band recorded it in twelve days with producer Ted Templeman. As a result there are five covers and many detours: jazz, country blues, doo-wop, a cappella and neoclassical. Dancing in the Street by Martha and the Vandellas also became a hit.

Cathedral is an instrumental piece in which Eddie Van Halen uses an echo effect to create a guitar sound that reminded the band of a church organ. Little Guitars was inspired by the flamenco guitarist Carlos Montoya. The album sold well, but critics at the time were less enthusiastic than they had been about its predecessor Fair Warning.
werk/van-halen-diver-down.listen: Listen to Cathedral and notice how the echo effect makes the guitar sound like a church organ and lets the notes flow on.

werk/van-halen-fair-warning.text:
Fair Warning was released in April 1981 as the band's fourth album, on Warner Bros. Records. The cover shows parts of The Maze, a painting by the Canadian artist William Kurelek about his hard childhood. The sleeve also contained a photograph of a wall with broken windows and a line from the opening song Mean Street, as graffiti.

The record reached number 5 on the Billboard 200, but it was the lowest-selling of the Roth years, and the single So This Is Love? did not make the Hot 100. The critical response was mostly positive. Robert Christgau heard a rhythm section that could handle punk speed, and Stephen Thomas Erlewine called it a dark, dirty and surly album with some of the hardest music the group ever made. Rolling Stone remarked that the synthesizer at the end of the record would return on later albums.
werk/van-halen-fair-warning.listen: Listen to Mean Street and notice how hard and dark the guitar and the rhythm section sound here.

werk/van-halen-jump.text: At the end of 1983, Van Halen's Jump was released, the band of guitarist Eddie Van Halen, one of the most influential guitarists of his time. It was he, of all people, who played the riff of Jump on a synthesizer, an Oberheim, instead of on the guitar. For some of the fans that was betrayal. Jump became the band's biggest hit, and their only number one in America. Once again the same question: adapt or stay true?
werk/van-halen-jump.listen: The riff does not come from the guitar, but from the Oberheim synthesizer. Only in the middle does the short, lightning-fast guitar solo arrive.

werk/van-halen-women-and-children-first.text:
Women and Children First was released in March 1980 as the group's third album, produced by Ted Templeman. It was recorded in about two weeks in Hollywood, at Sunset Studios, and for the first time contained no cover versions at all. More overdubs can be heard and there is less emphasis on backing vocals. Two songs, In a Simple Rhyme and Take Your Whiskey Home, had already been written six years earlier and recorded as demos. The opener And the Cradle Will Rock... sounds like a guitar, but is a Wurlitzer electric piano through a Marshall amplifier. In Could This Be Magic? Nicolette Larson sings along, the only female backing voice on a song by the band.

The reviews were mostly favourable and the record went platinum within a year. Critics heard a heavier and more serious group, and Rolling Stone and Kerrang! later put the album on their lists of the best metal albums.
werk/van-halen-women-and-children-first.listen: Listen to And the Cradle Will Rock... and notice the sound it begins with: it seems like a guitar, but is an electric piano.

werk/van-morrison-astral-weeks.text:
In early 1968, Van Morrison was stuck in a contract dispute with Bang Records, which meant he could not record. He played in clubs around Boston, first with a bassist and later with a flautist, in an acoustic line-up. Warner Bros. eventually signed him. Producer Lewis Merenstein brought jazz musicians to the Century Sound Studios in New York, including bassist Richard Davis, guitarist Jay Berliner and drummer Connie Kay.

The recording took place on 25 September and 1 and 15 October 1968. Morrison sang and played guitar in a separate booth while the band played together without scores. Strings and horns were added later, to his displeasure. The music mixes folk, blues, jazz and classical influences and differs greatly from his earlier pop success Brown Eyed Girl. The record initially failed to catch on, but grew into one of the most important albums in rock.
werk/van-morrison-astral-weeks.listen: In Astral Weeks, listen to how the acoustic guitar, the bass and the vocals sound together as a freely flowing whole, without a strict rhythm.

werk/van-morrison-blowin-your-mind.text:
Blowin' Your Mind! is Van Morrison's first solo record, released in 1967. He recorded the songs on 28 and 29 March 1967, intended for four separate singles. Producer Bert Berns put an album together from them without his consent. Shortly before, Morrison had signed a contract with Bang Records that deprived him of almost all control. He hated the psychedelic sleeve design, because it misrepresented his music.

The album contains Brown Eyed Girl, his first solo smash. T.B. Sheets is a long, drawn-out song, and He Ain't Give You None mentions places in London. AllMusic gave three stars and saw the record as a preliminary study for Astral Weeks. Rolling Stone placed it among the forty essential albums of 1967.
werk/van-morrison-blowin-your-mind.listen: Listen to Brown Eyed Girl and notice the backing vocals by The Sweet Inspirations.

werk/van-morrison-hard-nose-the-highway.text:
Hard Nose the Highway came out in 1973. The recording ran from August to November 1972, partly in a studio that Van Morrison had had built next to his house in Fairfax, California. According to him it was the first album that he produced entirely himself. Almost thirty songs came out of it, enough for a double album, but Warner Bros. managed to convince him of a single record. Some of the rest did not appear until 1998.

For the first time since his debut, the album also contains songs by others: Bein' Green, best known from Kermit the Frog, and the traditional Purple Heather. Snow in San Anselmo opens with the Oakland Symphony Chamber Chorus, and Warm Love became a successful single. The singer said that one side sounds hard and the other soft. The first reviews were full of praise, but later critics were less positive. The biographer Erik Hage thought the criticism unnecessary, because the album followed an exceptional run of records.
werk/van-morrison-hard-nose-the-highway.listen: In Snow in San Anselmo, listen to the choir that opens the song. Notice how Morrison paints the snow like a sketch in images.

werk/van-morrison-his-band-and-the-stree.text:
Van Morrison released this fourth album in November 1970 on Warner Bros. It was first called Virgo's Fool, but the label gave it another title without his consent. The recording began early in 1970 with a demo session in a small church in Woodstock. He then worked at A&R Studios in New York. He wanted to record the album a cappella, with just a vocal group that he called the Street Choir. In the end a band played too, and he was later dissatisfied with it.

Reviewers praised the free, relaxed sound, but found the lyrics simpler than on earlier work. The record reached number 32 on the Billboard 200. The success came mainly from Domino, which reached the American top ten. Blue Money and Call Me Up in Dreamland made the Billboard Hot 100.
werk/van-morrison-his-band-and-the-stree.listen: Listen to Domino and notice how vocals and band together carry the greatest success of his solo career.

werk/van-morrison-saint-dominic-s-previe.text:
Saint Dominic's Preview came about between late 1971 and the spring of 1972 in studios in San Francisco, with Ted Templeman as co-producer. Van Morrison's band constantly changed its line-up, and some of the musicians were new. Listen to the Lion was a leftover from the sessions for Tupelo Honey. Jackie Wilson Said (I'm in Heaven When You Smile) came from a single take: the band had little time to rehearse and the first take was used.

The album brings together Celtic folk, rhythm and blues, blues, jazz and singer-songwriter work. Jackie Wilson Said and the title track mix soul and folk. Listen to the Lion and Almost Independence Day are long songs with intense, almost raw vocals, comparable to Astral Weeks. Rolling Stone called it his best-produced and most ambitious record up to that point. It reached number 15 on the Billboard 200. Unlike with his two previous albums, the singer himself spoke well of it.
werk/van-morrison-saint-dominic-s-previe.listen: In Listen to the Lion, listen to the intense, almost raw vocals. Notice how long the song lasts and how the voice carries the tension.
